name: Uma Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a pick-and-place line at an electronics plant that makes circuit boards for boilers and washing machines. The pick-and-place machine is the one that grabs tiny parts off reels and puts them on the board, hundreds a minute. My job is loading the reels, checking the solder paste printer, clearing errors and pulling boards for inspection under the microscope. It's clean work, gowns and wrist straps, very different from what people imagine a factory to be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the little puzzles, like why the machine keeps dropping one resistor. I use an AI app on my phone every day to look up error codes and part numbers, faster than the manual. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than similar plants elsewhere, and the fact that there's only one plant like this within an hour. I share a flat with my friend Chiara, and I've got maybe two weeks' rent saved after paying off my scooter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not magic, which is what I've thought all along. At work I'd keep showing people the app tricks. Online I'd probably post something like 'told you, it's a tool'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly good news, because my job stays. But my pay doesn't go up, and there's still only one plant like ours nearby. So I'd still feel stuck, just not threatened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and keep learning, maybe the line technician course the plant offers once a year. I'd try to put a bit aside each month now that the scooter's paid off. I'd keep using AI for the error codes, because it saves me twenty minutes a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit restless, like I want more than this, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Would you keep doing that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Absolutely, it's like a calculator for me now. The AI app on my phone saves me twenty minutes a shift on error codes, and my supervisor still thinks I've memorised the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two weeks' rent saved. What would a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing overtime, mostly. If the boiler orders drop in summer, we lose Saturdays, and Saturdays are my rent margin. I'd have to borrow from my brother, which I hate.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but not magic**, as I always thought.
I'd keep showing colleagues the **app tricks** I use.
think: I think my **job stays**, which is mostly good news.
I think I'd still feel **stuck** on low pay with one plant nearby.
do: Apply for the **line technician course** the plant offers yearly.
Put money aside monthly now the **scooter** is paid off.
Keep using **AI for error codes**, saving twenty minutes a shift.
feel: **Fine** but restless, wanting more than this.
S0.quote: The AI app on my phone saves me twenty minutes a shift on error codes, and my supervisor still thinks I've memorised the manual.
fieldNote: Uma already uses AI **every day** as a practical shortcut.
Her pressure is **summer overtime cuts** and a two-week cushion.

steps.text: Apply for the plant's yearly line technician course
Save monthly now the scooter loan is paid off
Keep using the AI app for machine error codes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get skilled up, because the people who learn it will be fine. At work I'd volunteer to test anything new. Online I'd share how I'm using AI on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's a good picture for me if I'm quick. The inspection paperwork and the scheduling would move to software, and someone has to run that software on the floor. I'd want to be that person before they hire someone from outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to put me on the line technician course this year, not next. I'd learn the plant's new planning software in my own time. I'd keep a bit of money aside in case it goes the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection log and the reel ordering, I think, because that's typing and checking. If software does the inspection log at the electronics plant, I want to be the operator who knows how to fix the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the plant you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Giorgio, who's been there twenty years and won't touch a phone app. He's brilliant with the machines, but he'd struggle with the screens.

say: I'd say it's the moment to **get skilled up**, because people who learn will be fine.
I'd **volunteer** to test anything new at work and share my AI tricks online.
think: I think it's a **good picture** for me if I move quickly.
I think I want to run the **new software** before they hire someone outside.
do: Ask to join the **line technician course** this year.
Learn the plant's **planning software** in my own time.
Keep a little **money aside** in case it goes wrong.
S1.quote: If software does the inspection log at the electronics plant, I want to be the operator who knows how to fix the software.
fieldNote: Uma sees the **thinking tasks** on her line as an opening, not a threat.
She worries more about **Giorgio**, an older colleague, than herself.
Her only real fear here is **money**, given her thin cushion.

steps.text: Ask to join the line technician course this year
Learn the plant's new planning software in her own time
Keep a small emergency fund from her wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to move fast, and the government should help pay for it. At work I'd tell people to learn the robots now. Online I'd share anything useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit. The software side I was planning to move into goes first, in 2028, so my clever plan disappears. By 2031 the robots can load reels and clear errors too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch to robot maintenance, the hands-on side, because that has three more years. I'd look at moving to a city with more plants, even if rent is higher. I'd pick up weekend work, maybe fixing phones, to build a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. Like running on ice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots around 2031. You're quick with tech. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because I learn fast, but being quick doesn't help when the thing you're learning disappears. Being good with tech doesn't help much when the AI learns the machines faster than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fix phones for friends and neighbours at weekends, and save every bit I could. I'd tell Chiara we might need a cheaper flat.

say: I'd say everyone needs to **move fast**, with government help.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the **robots** now.
think: I think the **software side** I planned to join goes first.
I think by **2031** robots can do my job too.
do: Switch to **robot maintenance**, the hands-on side.
Look at **moving** to a city with more plants.
Fix **phones** at weekends to build cash.
S2.quote: Being good with tech doesn't help much when the AI learns the machines faster than I do.
fieldNote: Uma, normally confident, admits she's **more scared** than she'd say publicly.
The **thinking-first** order breaks her plan to move into software.
She'd consider **moving city** despite the rent, showing her appetite for risk.

steps.text: Retrain in robot maintenance instead of planning software
Look for jobs at electronics plants in bigger cities
Fix phones for neighbours at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be smart, not scared. At work I'd say start learning now. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is enough to become a line technician, earn more and save. Then I'd move into robot maintenance before the robots arrive. It's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the line technician course this year and the robot course after that. I'd save harder once my pay goes up. I'd stay where I am for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but realistic. I'd sleep okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, eight to the robots. What would you do in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two courses in five years, one after the other, and a pay rise in between. Five years is enough time for me to do two courses and get one pay rise before the robots arrive at the electronics plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still move cities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, if the plant didn't keep me. I'd rather stay near my family if I can.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people should be smart, not scared.
I'd tell colleagues to **start learning** now and share what I'm doing online.
think: I think five years is enough to become a **line technician**.
I think it's **tight but doable** before robots arrive.
do: Take the **line technician course** this year.
**Save harder** once my pay goes up.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to do two courses and get one pay rise before the robots arrive at the electronics plant.
fieldNote: Uma uses the years for a **two-step** plan: technician, then robot maintenance.
She'd stay near **family** unless forced to move.
She's **anxious** because her job still goes, though she feels in control.

steps.text: Complete the line technician course this year
Save more once the technician pay rise comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big chance, and people should use it. At work I'd say get trained while the company pays. Online I'd share my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine with ten years to plan. I'd become a technician, maybe a supervisor, and save properly for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the line technician course, then aim for a supervisor job in a few years. I'd save properly for the first time. I'd keep using AI tools as they get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A tiny worry for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. Does that feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very different, because I can plan instead of react. Ten years means I can plan my career at the electronics plant instead of reacting to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the line, or teaching new people how to work with the robots. I'd like that.

say: I'd say ten years is a **big chance**.
I'd tell colleagues to **get trained** while the company pays.
think: I think I'd be **fine** with ten years to plan.
I think I could become a **technician** or supervisor and save properly for once.
do: Aim for a **supervisor job** in a few years.
Keep using **AI tools** as they improve.
feel: **Calm**, with a tiny worry for later.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can plan my career at the electronics plant instead of reacting to it.
fieldNote: With a decade, Uma moves from survival to **career planning**.
She pictures herself **teaching** others to work with robots.
Thin savings keep a small **unease** even here.

steps.text: Apply for a line supervisor job within a few years
Use new AI tools on the line as they improve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan to move into software disappears and I've got no money to start again. What would help is paid training for robot maintenance and a bit of money for the gap. I'll learn anything you put in front of me, but I can't learn it for free on two weeks' rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in factories. Most of the line technicians at our plant are men, and the training mostly goes to them. I'd want that to change.

headlineQuote: I'll learn anything you put in front of me, but I can't learn it for free on two weeks' rent.
portrait: Uma, 27, runs a **pick-and-place line** at an electronics plant and shares a flat with two weeks' rent saved.
She uses **AI every day** for error codes and wants to move up to technician.
She's **pragmatic** and keen to learn, but her thin cushion limits how far she can jump.
She's **uneasy** in most pictures but **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when her software plan disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her plan to move into software disappears with no money to start again.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in robot maintenance and money to cover the gap.
